title: A Scalable Multi-Protocol Platform for Quantum Key Distribution Simulation with Rigorous Statistical Evaluation
abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) offers information- theoretically secure key establishment grounded in the laws of quantum physics, yet its practical reach is limited by the prohibitive cost of photonic hardware and the fragmented nature of existing simulation tools. Most simulators support only a single protocol and report results from individual stochastic runs, making systematic protocol comparison and reproducible statistical inference difficult. This paper presents a unified QKD simulation platform that implements four foundational protocols BB84, B92, E91, and BBM92 within a single Python/Qiskit engine. A shared impairment model covers fiber attenuation, source and detector losses, po- larization drift, and configurable intercept-resend eavesdropping. The platform is accessible through two independent interfaces that share the same backend: a desktop application (Tkinter, Matplotlib) for local experimentation and a browser-based web client (React, Node.js/Express) for zero-install remote access. All reported results are drawn from repeated-run studies (20 independent runs, 10000 qubits each), with mean, standard deviation, and 95% confidence intervals stated throughout. At a 25 km fiber link, BB84 achieves the highest mean key-rate of 160,045 Hz, followed by BBM92 (80023 Hz), E91 (52815 Hz), and B92 (40011 Hz) ordering that tracks simulation-derived sifting efficiencies precisely. Under the E91 protocol, the CHSH S-statistic averages 2.12 at baseline and falls to 1.58 when an eavesdropper is activated, demonstrating Bell-inequality-based intrusion detection independent of QBER
summary: This paper introduces a scalable, unified simulation platform for comparing four major Quantum Key Distribution protocols (BB84, B92, E91, BBM92). By modeling realistic channel impairments and performing extensive statistical analysis, it allows for systematic comparison of key rates and security diagnostics like the CHSH S-statistic across varying fiber lengths.
main_problem: Existing Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) simulation tools are limited to single protocols and lack rigorous statistical evaluation, hindering systematic comparison.
main_result: The platform demonstrates that BB84 achieves the highest mean key-rate (160,045 Hz) at 25 km, and the E91 protocol successfully detects eavesdropping by showing a drop in the CHSH S-statistic from 2.12 to 1.58.
method: The authors developed a unified simulation platform using Python/Qiskit that models four foundational QKD protocols (BB84, B92, E91, BBM92) under a shared impairment model.
model_or_system: The system simulates QKD over a fiber link, incorporating impairments like attenuation, source/detector losses, polarization drift, and configurable eavesdropping attacks. It supports both a local desktop GUI and a remote web client interface.
key_observables: Key-rate (Hz), Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER), and the CHSH S-statistic.
important_parameters: Fiber length (10, 25, 40 km), number of independent runs (20), and qubits per run (10000).
main_assumptions: The model primarily includes intercept-resend attacks; it does not account for dark counts, timing jitter, or multi-photon emission.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the desktop GUI for parameter entry and results visualization, and the web interface for parameter sweeps, showing confidence bands widening at longer distances.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the unified simulation platform architecture (Python/Qiskit core, dual interfaces), presents the shared impairment model, and concludes with comparative results across the four protocols and varying link lengths.
why_interesting: It provides a highly rigorous, statistically robust simulation environment for comparing fundamental quantum communication protocols, which is crucial for understanding practical quantum network feasibility.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Desktop GUI: single-simulation parameter panel. Every field carries a physical unit label. The eavesdropping checkbox and impairment toggles appear below the channel parameters. Range validation prevents values outside physically meaningful bounds before the run is dispatched (https://qkd-simulator-voe2.onrender.com/).

Fig. 2. Desktop GUI: per-protocol result cards from a single simulation pass. All four protocols execute in one call under identical parameters. The E91 card includes the CHSH S-statistic alongside the metrics shared by all protocols. The side-by-side layout makes sifting efficiency differences immediately visible (https://qkd-simulator-voe2.onrender.com/).
Fig. 1 shows the desktop parameter entry panel and Fig. 2 shows the per-protocol result cards generated after a single run. Figs. 3 and 4 show the corresponding web interface panels.

Fig. 3. Web interface: parameter sweep configuration panel. The user selects the sweep axis (here, fiber loss in dB/km), the range, step size, and number of runs per point. The form posts to /simulate/sweep; the server aggregates results before responding.

Fig. 4. Web interface: sweep results for all four protocols. Confidence bands (shaded) widen at 40 km due to detection sparsity under high attenuation. The protocol ordering is stable across all sweep points and consistent with the sifting coefficients in Table III.
